entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Paolo Emili (c. 1455 – May 5, 1529), known by his Latinized name Paulus Aemilius Veronensis, was a pioneering Italian Renaissance historian whose monumental *De rebus gestis Francorum* established a new standard for national historiography in early modern Europe. Commissioned by King Louis XII of France in 1499 and continued by Francis I, Emili's work marked a critical transition from medieval chronicles to humanistic historical analysis, focusing on critical source evaluation and a more polished, classical Latin style. His scholarship, rooted in Verona before his move to France, profoundly influenced the conceptualization of national identity through a historical narrative that sought to legitimize French monarchy and its imperial ambitions.

Emili dedicated the final three decades of his life to the *De rebus gestis Francorum*, a comprehensive history of the Franks and the French kings from their mythical origins to his own time. He meticulously consulted ancient charters, royal annals, and ecclesiastical records, often critically reassessing traditional narratives. His methodology involved synthesizing disparate sources, presenting a coherent chronological account, and injecting humanist rhetorical flourishes. Though unfinished at his death, with the work concluding in the reign of Charles VIII (1483-1498), it spanned the reigns of 63 kings, providing a foundational text for subsequent French historical scholarship and royal propaganda.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Paolo Emili's *De rebus gestis Francorum* redefined national historiography, influencing the writing of history across Europe and contributing to the formation of French national identity for centuries. His work served as a critical bridge between medieval chronicles and modern historical scholarship.
